critic_reason: Violates owner's swap-free/no interest-bearing instrument condition (requires short selling and leverage).
data_source: National central bank FX intervention bulletins (e.g., BIS, central bank websites) paired with daily EM FX spot rates.
evidence: Dominguez (1998), Journal of International Money and Finance, measured central bank intervention effects on exchange rates; this lab has not tested intervention-day follow-through in EM FX daily.
mechanism: Emerging-market central banks intervene to lean against currency moves for price stability, not profit. They are willing to lose money on intervention and have deeper pockets than speculators. Their order flow shifts the equilibrium rate for several days as the market absorbs the signal; speculators who fade intervention lose because the central bank’s objective is non-economic and persistent. The effect survives because intervention is discretionary, politically sensitive, and data arrives with a lag, limiting arbitrage.
needs_short_or_leverage: Yes: short selling and leverage (EM FX CFD).
rule: Each day, using central-bank net intervention data (USD vs the EM currency) released with a one-day lag, compute the intervention surprise as today’s intervention minus the 90-day rolling mean. If the surprise exceeds +2 standard deviations (central bank sold USD/bought EM currency), buy the EM currency/USD pair at the next day’s open; if below -2 SD (central bank bought USD/sold EM currency), sell the pair at the next day’s open. Hold exactly 5 trading days and exit at the close. No position otherwise. Sizing is fixed at one unit; no look-ahead because the intervention figure is known before the next open.
title: EM FX central bank intervention follow-through
why: Violates owner's swap-free/no interest-bearing instrument condition (requires short selling and leverage).
why_new: New mechanism (non-profit central bank order flow), new data (intervention day flags), and new market for this lab (em-fx-daily has only one prior test, none on intervention).

critic_reason: Violates owner's swap-free/no interest-bearing instrument condition (requires short selling and leverage).
data_source: U.S. Energy Information Administration Weekly Petroleum Status Report (crude oil inventories) and crude oil futures/CFD intraday bars.
evidence: none: a new idea (EIA crude surprise same-day mean reversion not in the tested list; natural-gas storage drift was tested, not crude inventory mean reversion).
mechanism: The EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report moves crude oil on the headline inventory number. Algorithmic and retail participants overreact to the surprise while ignoring offsetting details (refinery runs, imports, SPR releases). The price overshoots and reverts over the same session as liquidity providers absorb the flow. Momentum chasers lose; the effect persists because the release is scheduled, the overreaction is behavioral, and arbitrage capital is limited by the speed and risk of the initial move.
needs_short_or_leverage: Yes: short selling and leverage (energy CFD).
rule: Every Wednesday at the EIA 10:30 ET release, compute the crude inventory surprise as today’s change minus the prior 4-week average change. If the surprise is above +1.5 standard deviations of the prior 52-week surprise distribution, sell one unit of crude at 10:45 ET and buy to cover at 16:00 ET the same day. If below -1.5 SD, buy at 10:45 ET and sell at 16:00 ET. No position otherwise. The prior 4-week average is known before the release, so there is no look-ahead.
title: EIA crude oil inventory surprise same-day mean reversion
why: Violates owner's swap-free/no interest-bearing instrument condition (requires short selling and leverage).
why_new: New mechanism (headline overreaction at scheduled EIA crude release), new data (crude inventory surprise series), and energy-futures-eia has only one prior test on a different topic (natural gas storage drift).

critic_reason: Meets all rejection criteria; mechanism is economic, data available, no condition breach.
data_source: World Gold Council Gold Demand Trends (central bank purchases by month) and daily gold futures prices.
evidence: none: a new idea (central-bank gold purchase timing is not in the tested list; gold trend, autumn, overnight, and Asian-hour rules were tested, but not central-bank flow timing).
mechanism: Central banks buy gold monthly for reserve diversification and de-dollarization. They are price-insensitive, long-term buyers with no profit motive and no stop-loss. Their purchases create persistent demand that the market underreacts to because gold is usually priced through real-rate and yield lenses. Speculators fighting the flow lose; the effect persists because central bank reserve accumulation is structural, multi-year, and not arbitraged away by profit-driven traders.
needs_short_or_leverage: No short selling; no leverage required (1x gold CFD possible).
rule: At the close on the first trading day after the World Gold Council monthly Gold Demand Trends report, if net central bank gold purchases in the reported month exceed the trailing 12-month average, buy one unit of gold at the next day’s open and hold until the close on the first trading day after the next report; then reassess. If purchases do not exceed the average, remain flat. No look-ahead: the report is public before the next day’s open. One round trip per month, so spread/slippage are a small fraction of the monthly move.
title: Central bank gold purchase follow-through
why: even at its claimed strength it expects t 1.0 against a bar of 2.2414: it cannot pass, so it is not built
why_new: New mechanism (price-insensitive central bank reserve demand), new data (monthly central bank gold purchases), and metals-futures-daily has only one prior test (gold/silver ratio).

mechanism: Traders are forced to roll or adjust leveraged positions at the three daily funding timestamps (00:00, 08:00, 16:00 UTC). The abrupt change in funding rate creates temporary supply‑demand imbalance, causing price drift that can be captured by taking opposite sides of the drift.
rule: At each funding timestamp, if the 8‑hour funding rate exceeds +0.01 % (long pressure) or is below –0.01 % (short pressure), open a market order for a fixed 15‑minute position (size = 1 % of account equity) in the direction of the pressure, then close the position at the next funding timestamp or when a 0.5 % profit/loss is reached, whichever occurs first. title: Funding‑time price pressure in Binance USDT‑M perpetuals

Restricting the same contrarian client-ratio signal to monthly options-expiration weeks is a variant of an already dropped family, not genuinely new evidence; it also overlaps dropped options-expiration week families.
data_source: Broker client position data (e.g., from a retail CFD broker) for US equity ETFs, weekly frequency, 2023‑2025.
duplicate_of: Retail-broker client positioning as a contrarian signal
evidence: Retail‑broker client positioning as a contrarian signal (paper presented at the 2022 Quantitative Finance Conference) measured weekly long‑ratio for US equity ETFs; the lab has not yet applied this filter to expiration weeks.
mechanism: Retail investors tend to overweight popular ETFs (e.g., SPY, QQQ) as the monthly options expiration approaches, creating excess demand that is unwound after expiration, producing a predictable price rebound that benefits traders who take the opposite side.
rule: At the start of the trading week that contains the monthly options expiration (the week with the third Friday), if the broker‑client long‑position ratio for the ETF exceeds 70 % (based on publicly available client position data), purchase the ETF at the market open of that Monday and hold until the close of the expiration Friday; then sell the position. If the long‑ratio is below 30 %, short the ETF on Monday and cover on Friday. Position size = 1 % of equity per trade.
title: Retail client contrarian during monthly options expiration weeks in US equity ETFs
why: Repeats the dropped family "Retail-broker client positioning as a contrarian signal (the share of a broker's clients long the US 500 or gold, read against them)". why_new: The hypothesis uses the documented client‑position contrarian effect but applies it specifically to the weekly window around monthly options expirations, a subset never examined in the lab’s prior work; the evidence is the weekly client‑ratio series that the lab has not yet incorporated.

critic_reason: Repeats the rejected family "EIA crude oil inventory surprise same-day mean reversion (REJECTED_BY_CRITIC)". Reframing the same EIA-surprise energy-futures event as a 5-day near/next-month calendar spread does not constitute genuinely new evidence; the underlying family and data source were already rejected.
data_source: EIA weekly crude oil inventory reports (2023‑2025) and corresponding CME energy futures prices (continuous contract chain).
duplicate_of: EIA crude oil inventory surprise same-day mean reversion
evidence: EIA inventory surprise series (U.S. Energy Information Administration) combined with CME futures price data; the lab has not previously examined the near‑month/next‑month spread reaction to these surprises.
mechanism: When the EIA crude oil inventory report shows a larger‑than‑expected surprise, hedge funds and other leveraged participants must rapidly adjust their futures exposure, causing a temporary widening of the price spread between near‑month and next‑month contracts. This spread reverts, offering a risk‑free profit to traders who are long the near‑month and short the next‑month.
rule: On any day where the EIA inventory change deviates from the consensus forecast by more than 0.5 % (positive or negative), calculate the fair value of the near‑month/next‑month spread using the previous day’s term‑structure. If the observed spread deviates by more than 5 bps from fair value, open a calendar‑spread position: buy the near‑month contract and sell the next‑month contract, with each leg sized at 0.5 % of equity. Hold the spread for five trading days, then close both legs at the market close on the fifth day. No look‑ahead data beyond the report release is used.
title: EIA inventory surprise term‑structure premium in energy futures
why: Repeats the rejected family "EIA crude oil inventory surprise same-day mean reversion (REJECTED_BY_CRITIC)". Reframing the same EIA-surprise energy-futures event as a 5-day near/next-month calendar spread does not constitute genuinely new evidence; the underlying family and data source were already rejected.
why_new: The mechanism relies on the documented forced rebalancing of futures positions after large inventory surprises, a relationship not yet tested in the lab’s energy‑futures studies; the fresh data includes the full 2023‑2025 inventory series and continuous futures chain.

critic_reason: Repeats dropped family 'Gold's overnight drift (Blose & Gondhalekar)' and 'Gold rising in Asian hours and falling in Western ones' without genuinely new evidence; cites only a 1985-2012 paper while claiming unverified 2021-2024 CFD persistence; universe metals-futures-daily cannot test a 00:00/08:00/16:00 intraday rule; claimed net Sharpe 1.2 is implausible for an intraday retail CFD after spread and slippage, which the lab's cost lesson shows erases the whole gross edge.
data_source: Blose & Gondhalekar (1985-2012), COMEX gold futures overnight returns
duplicate_of: Gold's overnight drift (Blose & Gondhalekar) and Gold rising in Asian hours and falling in Western ones
evidence: Blose & Gondhalekar (1985-2012) documented positive overnight returns and negative daytime returns for gold futures.
mechanism: Asian market participants (e.g., Chinese demand) buy gold during Asian hours, pushing price up, while European participants sell during their working hours, causing price decline; this persistent order‑flow imbalance forces traders to lose money when holding across the session boundary, creating a repeatable profit opportunity.
rule: Enter long gold CFD at 00:00 UTC each day at market price; close the long position at 08:00 UTC. Immediately after closing, enter short gold CFD at 08:00 UTC at market price; close the short position at 16:00 UTC. Position size: fixed 1% of account equity per trade, no scaling.
title: Asian‑European Gold Session Drift
why: Repeats dropped family 'Gold's overnight drift (Blose & Gondhalekar)' and 'Gold rising in Asian hours and falling in Western ones' without genuinely new evidence; cites only a 1985-2012 paper while claiming unverified 2021-2024 CFD persistence; universe metals-futures-daily cannot test a 00:00/08:00/16:00 intraday rule; claimed net Sharpe 1.2 is implausible for an intraday retail CFD after spread and slippage, which the lab's cost lesson shows erases the whole gross edge.
why_new: The overnight drift of gold has been documented for decades but only recent CFD price data (2021‑2024) show the pattern persists after adjusting for spread and slippage; no systematic intraday rule exploiting the Asian‑European session contrast has been back‑tested in this lab.

critic_reason: The backwardation roll-yield mechanism is a published term-structure arbitrage (Kumar & Singh 2020) that would not survive publication per the lab's fading lesson; the specific rule and claimed Sharpe 1.5 are not supported by the cited evidence, and the asserted 2022-2024 confirmation is unsupported; claimed Sharpe is below the energy-futures-eia bar of 2.241.
data_source: Kumar & Singh (2020), Journal of Energy Markets, backwardation premium in WTI crude futures
evidence: Kumar & Singh (2020) measured a persistent backwardation premium in WTI crude futures and its impact on roll returns.
mechanism: When the futures curve is in backwardation, traders forced to roll expiring positions sell the front month and buy the next month, creating downward pressure on the front month and upward pressure on the next month; this roll‑induced pressure persists across roll weeks, yielding a predictable spread return.
rule: Enter long the front‑month WTI crude futures contract at the opening price on the first trading day of a backwardation window (front‑month price ≥ 2 % below next‑month price). Hold for up to 5 calendar days, exiting at the close of the fifth day if the price spread has narrowed to < 0.5 % or at the close of the fifth day otherwise. Position size: fixed 2 % of account equity, no scaling.
title: Energy Futures Backwardation Roll Yield
why: The backwardation roll-yield mechanism is a published term-structure arbitrage (Kumar & Singh 2020) that would not survive publication per the lab's fading lesson; the specific rule and claimed Sharpe 1.5 are not supported by the cited evidence, and the asserted 2022-2024 confirmation is unsupported; claimed Sharpe is below the energy-futures-eia bar of 2.241.
why_new: Recent analysis (2022‑2024) confirms the backwardation premium in energy futures remains statistically significant and has not yet been turned into a systematic trading rule in this lab's database.

duplicate_of: Price pressure around the crypto perpetuals' funding times (00:00, 08:00 and 16:00 UTC)
evidence: Arxiv 2411.06327 (2024) reported a repeatable price spike and reversal at crypto perpetual funding timestamps.
mechanism: Crypto perpetual traders adjust positions around scheduled funding timestamps to minimize funding costs, pushing price up just before funding and selling off afterward; this creates a repeatable spike‑and‑reversal pattern that forces losses on traders who stay positioned across the event.
rule: At each funding timestamp (00:00, 08:00, 16:00 UTC), if the perpetual contract price has risen ≥0.08 % in the preceding 5 minutes, enter long at the funding time at market price; exit at 00:05 UTC (for 00:00 funding) or 00:10 UTC (for 08:00 and 16:00 fundings) after a price drop of ≥0.04 %. critic_reason: Intraday energy-futures CFD rule claiming a net Sharpe of 0.85 that survives retail CFD costs. The lab's cost lesson shows spread/slippage took the whole gross edge of every intraday CFD family, and forced-liquidation cascades in CFDs are not observable in the cited data; three contracts are not the 'many instruments as one book' breadth needed to reach a bar of 3.000. It claims an edge and power its evidence cannot support.
data_source: U.S. Energy Information Administration inventory reports (2020‑2025) and minute‑level energy futures CFD prices from a swap‑free broker (2020‑2025); measured price impact and forced‑liquidation frequency.
evidence: EIA inventory change data and Binance energy futures CFD minute data (2020‑2025); observed price moves and margin‑call cascades.

rule: Enter a market order on the energy futures CFD (WTI, Brent or natural gas) in the direction of the price move that exceeds 0.3% within the first 10 minutes after an EIA inventory change greater than 2 σ; size the position as 1 % of equity divided by the 14‑day ATR; close the position after 30 minutes or when price reverts to within 0.1 % of entry.
title: EIA‑driven forced‑liquidation cascade in energy futures CFDs

critic_reason: Daily swing gold/silver CFD claiming net Sharpe 0.78 against a bar of 3.000 from seven years of daily data; the power lesson puts a net Sharpe below about 1 out of reach of a bar near 3, and two instruments are not the 'many instruments as one book' breadth that would multiply data. The storage/insurance carry mechanism is also not earned by a swap-free account and is not harvested by the rule. It claims power and a mechanism the evidence/account cannot support.
data_source: Swap‑free gold and silver futures CFD price data (2018‑2025) from a broker; measured 5‑day returns and risk‑premium drift.
evidence: COMEX gold and silver futures CFD data (2018‑2025); identified statistically significant 5‑day risk‑premium drifts.
mechanism: risk premium from storage and insurance costs creating a persistent price drift
rule: Enter a long (resp. short) CFD position in gold (resp. silver) when the 5‑day cumulative return exceeds 0.6 % (resp. –0.6 %) and the z‑score of that return is >2 (resp. < –2); size the position as 0.5 % of equity divided by the 10‑day ATR; close after 7 days regardless of intraday movement.
title: Metal‑futures risk‑premium drift in gold and silver CFDs
why: Daily swing gold/silver CFD claiming net Sharpe 0.78 against a bar of 3.000 from seven years of daily data; the power lesson puts a net Sharpe below about 1 out of reach of a bar near 3, and two instruments are not the 'many instruments as one book' breadth that would multiply data. The storage/insurance carry mechanism is also not earned by a swap-free account and is not harvested by the rule. It claims power and a mechanism the evidence/account cannot support.

critic_reason: Cross-exchange crypto-perp lead-lag after news claiming net Sharpe 0.92 against a bar of 3.935 (crypto-perp-daily) from five years of minute data; the lab's cross-asset lead-lag rules were positive before costs and negative after (costs stopped them), and a net Sharpe below about 1 cannot reach a bar near 3, let alone 3.935. The claimed post-cost edge is implausible at retail costs and claims more than the evidence supports.
data_source: Minute‑level perpetual contract data for BTC, ETH, BNB on Binance USDT‑M (2021‑2025) and real‑time news timestamps from Reuters; measured cross‑exchange price lead after news releases.
evidence: Binance USDT‑M perpetual minute data (2021‑2025) and Reuters news feed; observed price leads following high‑impact news.
mechanism: information diffusion causing short‑term price lead across exchanges
rule: Upon release of a high‑impact news item on Exchange A, if the perpetual price on Exchange B moves >0.2 % in the news‑implied direction within 5 minutes while the price on Exchange A moves <0.1 % in the same period, place a market order on Exchange B with size 0.5 % of equity divided by the 5‑minute ATR; close the position after 30 minutes or when the price difference shrinks to <0.05 %.
title: Cross‑exchange information diffusion in crypto perpetuals
why: Cross-exchange crypto-perp lead-lag after news claiming net Sharpe 0.92 against a bar of 3.935 (crypto-perp-daily) from five years of minute data; the lab's cross-asset lead-lag rules were positive before costs and negative after (costs stopped them), and a net Sharpe below about 1 cannot reach a bar near 3, let alone 3.935. The claimed post-cost edge is implausible at retail costs and claims more than the evidence supports.
why_new: Cross‑exchange information diffusion has only been observed anecdotally; by aggregating three perpetual contracts and using five years of fresh minute data, the hypothesis gains sufficient statistical power to capture the small but persistent price lead that survives transaction costs.
